title: ISACA Certified in Risk and Information Systems Control (CRISC)

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: During a risk assessment, the practitioner determines that a critical legacy application has a HIGH likelihood of failure and would cause SEVERE business impact, but remediation would cost more than the asset's value. Which response is MOST appropriate to recommend?
choices: Accept the risk and continue operating the application as-is
Transfer the risk through cyber insurance covering downtime
Avoid the risk by retiring the application and migrating users
Mitigate the risk with additional preventive controls regardless of cost
questions.explanation: When a risk is high-likelihood and high-impact and mitigation is not cost-effective, CRISC favours risk avoidance — eliminating the activity that creates the exposure. Retiring the application removes the source of the risk entirely. Acceptance is inappropriate because the impact is severe, insurance does not address operational loss adequately, and over-controlling an asset worth less than the controls violates the cost-benefit principle.

questions.q: Senior management decides to formally accept a residual risk that exceeds the documented risk tolerance. What is the risk practitioner's MOST appropriate action?
choices: Override management and implement additional controls anyway
Document the acceptance, ensure it is approved at the appropriate authority level, and schedule periodic review
Remove the risk from the risk register since it has been accepted
Report the issue directly to external regulators
questions.explanation: When management accepts risk above tolerance, the practitioner's role is to ensure governance — not to override the business. CRISC requires that the acceptance be formally documented, approved by an authority level appropriate to the magnitude (often the board for out-of-tolerance items), justified, time-bounded, and re-reviewed periodically. Removing the risk from the register hides exposure, escalating to regulators bypasses internal governance, and overriding management exceeds the practitioner's mandate.

questions.q: A penetration test discovers a critical vulnerability in a production application, but patching requires a maintenance window that the business will not approve for two weeks. Which action BEST balances risk and business needs in the interim?
choices: Take the application offline until the patch can be applied
Accept the risk silently since a patch date is already scheduled
Implement a compensating control such as a virtual patch on the WAF and document the temporary exception
Inform the business that the patch will be applied without their approval
questions.explanation: CRISC defines compensating controls as alternative measures that reduce exposure when the primary control cannot be implemented immediately. A virtual patch on a web application firewall (WAF) blocks exploitation of the vulnerability at the perimeter while the underlying code is fixed on the agreed schedule. Silent acceptance, taking down production, and bypassing business approval each violate either risk-management discipline or governance.

questions.q: A newly identified risk exceeds the organization's risk appetite. The business owner wants to accept it because the treatment cost is high. Who has the authority to formally accept a risk that is above appetite?
choices: The IT security team, since they identified the risk.
Any employee who documents the decision in the risk register.
The internal audit function, as an independent party.
Appropriate senior management/risk owner with the authority for that risk level, following the governance escalation path.
questions.explanation: Accepting a risk that breaches appetite is a governance decision reserved for management with authority commensurate with the risk — often escalated to senior leadership or the board per the risk-acceptance framework. Security identifies and advises but does not own acceptance, audit must stay independent and cannot own risk decisions, and documentation in the register does not by itself confer acceptance authority.

questions.q: Management decides to move a data-processing activity to a third party to reduce operational risk. In risk-response terms, which statement is MOST accurate?
choices: The risk is eliminated because a third party now performs the activity.
Outsourcing is always cheaper and therefore always the correct response.
This is risk avoidance and no further monitoring is needed.
This is risk transfer/sharing, but accountability for the risk remains with the organization and new third-party risks are introduced.
questions.explanation: Outsourcing shares or transfers some risk, but the organization stays accountable for the outcome and must now manage vendor/third-party risk (and any residual). It does not eliminate risk (that would require ceasing the activity — avoidance), monitoring is still required, and cost is not a guaranteed benefit or the basis for the response.

questions.q: After treatment, a residual risk still sits slightly above appetite, and further controls would cost far more than the expected loss. What is the MOST appropriate recommendation?
choices: Implement the expensive control anyway to reach zero risk.
Transfer the risk to insurance regardless of terms.
Lower the documented risk rating so it appears within appetite.
Escalate for a formal risk-acceptance decision by the appropriate authority, documenting the cost-benefit rationale and monitoring plan.
questions.explanation: When treatment cost outweighs the benefit but residual is above appetite, the right path is a documented, formal acceptance by the authority that owns the risk, supported by cost-benefit rationale and ongoing monitoring. Spending more than the risk is worth is not cost-effective, manipulating the rating is unethical and defeats governance, and insurance should be chosen on its merits, not as a reflex.

nodes.title: Risk Monitoring: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Risk Monitoring. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A risk committee is confused because a metric labeled a KRI on one report appears as a KPI on another, and asks the practitioner to clarify the distinction. Which of the following BEST differentiates a key risk indicator (KRI) from a key performance indicator (KPI)?
flashcards.back: CRISC defines a KRI as a leading, predictive metric whose movement warns that risk exposure is changing — for example, a rising count of failed privileged logins suggesting credential compromise. A KPI is a lagging measure of how well an objective has already been met. Both can be quantitative, reported at any level, and tracked at any cadence; the defining distinction is leading risk signal vs. lagging performance result.

flashcards.front: An IT risk register entry has been open for 18 months with no risk-response action taken and no formal acceptance documented. What is the MOST appropriate next step for the risk practitioner?
flashcards.back: Open risks without action or acceptance are governance failures. The practitioner's role is to re-evaluate whether the original assessment still holds, then escalate to a sufficiently senior owner who must either approve a treatment plan with deadlines or formally accept the risk through the documented exception process. Silently closing or deleting the entry hides exposure, and shifting it to audit confuses the second and third lines of defence.

flashcards.front: A control has been implemented to treat a risk. Which metric BEST tells management whether the control is continuing to operate effectively over time?
flashcards.back: A key control indicator monitored continuously against a threshold signals when a control's effectiveness degrades, enabling timely response — the purpose of ongoing risk monitoring. A single go-live pen test is a point-in-time check, the implementation budget measures spend not effectiveness, and training attendance is an activity metric, not evidence the control still works.

flashcards.front: A risk practitioner is building a risk register entry. Which combination BEST expresses the risk so it can be prioritized and tracked?
flashcards.back: A useful register entry describes the full scenario (what could happen to which asset via which weakness, and the business impact) plus likelihood, impact, existing controls, and an accountable owner — everything needed to prioritize and track it. A vague label, a lone control name, or just a discovery date cannot be assessed or assigned.

questions.q: A risk committee is confused because a metric labeled a KRI on one report appears as a KPI on another, and asks the practitioner to clarify the distinction. Which of the following BEST differentiates a key risk indicator (KRI) from a key performance indicator (KPI)?
choices: A KRI is measured monthly while a KPI is measured quarterly
A KRI is forward-looking and signals changing risk exposure, while a KPI measures historical performance against an objective
A KRI is qualitative while a KPI is always quantitative
A KRI is reported to the board while a KPI is reported to management
questions.explanation: CRISC defines a KRI as a leading, predictive metric whose movement warns that risk exposure is changing — for example, a rising count of failed privileged logins suggesting credential compromise. A KPI is a lagging measure of how well an objective has already been met. Both can be quantitative, reported at any level, and tracked at any cadence; the defining distinction is leading risk signal vs. lagging performance result.

questions.q: An IT risk register entry has been open for 18 months with no risk-response action taken and no formal acceptance documented. What is the MOST appropriate next step for the risk practitioner?
choices: Close the entry on the grounds that no incident has materialised
Re-evaluate the risk, escalate the stalled response to an appropriate authority, and obtain either an updated treatment plan or formal acceptance
Delete the entry and create a new one with a fresh identifier
Reassign ownership of the entry to the internal audit function
questions.explanation: Open risks without action or acceptance are governance failures. The practitioner's role is to re-evaluate whether the original assessment still holds, then escalate to a sufficiently senior owner who must either approve a treatment plan with deadlines or formally accept the risk through the documented exception process. Silently closing or deleting the entry hides exposure, and shifting it to audit confuses the second and third lines of defence.

questions.q: A control has been implemented to treat a risk. Which metric BEST tells management whether the control is continuing to operate effectively over time?
choices: A key control indicator (KCI) tracked on an ongoing basis against a defined threshold.
A one-time penetration test performed at go-live.
The original project budget for implementing the control.
The number of employees who attended the control's training session.
questions.explanation: A key control indicator monitored continuously against a threshold signals when a control's effectiveness degrades, enabling timely response — the purpose of ongoing risk monitoring. A single go-live pen test is a point-in-time check, the implementation budget measures spend not effectiveness, and training attendance is an activity metric, not evidence the control still works.

questions.q: A risk practitioner is building a risk register entry. Which combination BEST expresses the risk so it can be prioritized and tracked?
choices: The risk scenario (threat, vulnerability, asset, and business impact) with likelihood, impact, current controls, and a named risk owner.
A generic label such as 'cyber risk — high.'
Only the name of the control that will be applied.
The date the risk was discovered and nothing more.
questions.explanation: A useful register entry describes the full scenario (what could happen to which asset via which weakness, and the business impact) plus likelihood, impact, existing controls, and an accountable owner — everything needed to prioritize and track it. A vague label, a lone control name, or just a discovery date cannot be assessed or assigned.

questions.q: A key risk indicator (KRI) has been chosen for a critical risk. Which characteristic is MOST important for it to be effective?
choices: It should be easy to collect even if it is only loosely related to the risk.
It should always trend upward to show progress.
It should be a leading, measurable indicator that reliably signals a change in the risk level in time to act.
It should be reported once a year to reduce noise.
questions.explanation: An effective KRI is measurable and predictive — ideally leading — so a change in it gives management enough warning to respond before the risk materializes. Ease of collection matters only if the indicator is actually relevant, a KRI is not meant to always rise, and annual reporting is far too infrequent to enable timely action on a critical risk.

nodes.title: Risk Assessment: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Risk Assessment. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A risk practitioner is calculating annualised loss expectancy (ALE) for a ransomware scenario. Single loss expectancy (SLE) is $500,000 and the annual rate of occurrence (ARO) is 0.2. What is the ALE?
flashcards.back: ALE is calculated as SLE × ARO. With SLE of $500,000 and ARO of 0.2 (a one-in-five-year event), ALE = $500,000 × 0.2 = $100,000. This figure is the expected annualised loss before controls and is the quantitative basis for justifying control investments — a mitigating control whose annualised cost is below $100,000 generally produces a positive return.

flashcards.front: A practitioner must explain to business owners how the controls they operate change the organization's exposure to a given threat. Which of the following BEST describes the relationship between inherent risk, control effectiveness, and residual risk?
flashcards.back: Inherent risk is the risk that exists before any controls are considered. Once controls are applied, they reduce — but rarely eliminate — that exposure; the portion that remains is the residual risk. CRISC frames the relationship conceptually rather than as a fixed arithmetic formula, because control effectiveness is rarely a clean percentage. Residual risk is what the practitioner compares against the risk appetite to decide whether further response is required.

flashcards.front: During quantitative risk analysis, a single-loss expectancy (SLE) is $50,000 and the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) is 0.2. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE), and how should it be used?
flashcards.back: ALE = SLE × ARO = $50,000 × 0.2 = $10,000. It represents the expected yearly loss and is compared with the annualized cost of a control to decide whether the control is economically justified (a control costing more than $10,000/yr to address this risk is hard to justify on ALE alone). $250,000 and dividing SLE by ARO are wrong arithmetic, and ignoring frequency (using the full SLE) overstates the annual expectation.

flashcards.front: During a control review a practitioner must clearly separate the exposure that exists before controls from what remains after they operate, so management can compare it to appetite. Which statement about inherent versus residual risk is correct?
flashcards.back: Inherent risk is the level of exposure before considering controls; residual risk is what remains after controls operate, and it is the residual figure that management compares to appetite to decide on further treatment. They are not equal when controls have effect, and while residual is normally below inherent, poorly designed or failed controls can leave residual effectively unchanged — so 'never higher' is not a reliable absolute.

questions.q: A risk practitioner is calculating annualised loss expectancy (ALE) for a ransomware scenario. Single loss expectancy (SLE) is $500,000 and the annual rate of occurrence (ARO) is 0.2. What is the ALE?
questions.explanation: ALE is calculated as SLE × ARO. With SLE of $500,000 and ARO of 0.2 (a one-in-five-year event), ALE = $500,000 × 0.2 = $100,000. This figure is the expected annualised loss before controls and is the quantitative basis for justifying control investments — a mitigating control whose annualised cost is below $100,000 generally produces a positive return.

questions.q: A practitioner must explain to business owners how the controls they operate change the organization's exposure to a given threat. Which of the following BEST describes the relationship between inherent risk, control effectiveness, and residual risk?
choices: Residual risk = inherent risk + control effectiveness
Residual risk = inherent risk × control effectiveness
Residual risk is the portion of inherent risk that remains after controls are applied
Residual risk is unrelated to inherent risk and is set by management
questions.explanation: Inherent risk is the risk that exists before any controls are considered. Once controls are applied, they reduce — but rarely eliminate — that exposure; the portion that remains is the residual risk. CRISC frames the relationship conceptually rather than as a fixed arithmetic formula, because control effectiveness is rarely a clean percentage. Residual risk is what the practitioner compares against the risk appetite to decide whether further response is required.

questions.q: During quantitative risk analysis, a single-loss expectancy (SLE) is $50,000 and the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) is 0.2. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE), and how should it be used?
choices: $250,000 — spend up to that amount on any control.
$2,500 — divide SLE by ARO to get the annual figure.
$50,000 — the full SLE is the annual expected loss regardless of frequency.
$10,000 — compare it against the annual cost of a proposed control to judge cost-effectiveness.
questions.explanation: ALE = SLE × ARO = $50,000 × 0.2 = $10,000. It represents the expected yearly loss and is compared with the annualized cost of a control to decide whether the control is economically justified (a control costing more than $10,000/yr to address this risk is hard to justify on ALE alone). $250,000 and dividing SLE by ARO are wrong arithmetic, and ignoring frequency (using the full SLE) overstates the annual expectation.

questions.q: During a control review a practitioner must clearly separate the exposure that exists before controls from what remains after they operate, so management can compare it to appetite. Which statement about inherent versus residual risk is correct?
choices: Inherent risk is the risk remaining after controls; residual is before controls.
Residual risk can never be higher than inherent risk under any circumstance.
Inherent and residual risk are always equal.
Inherent risk is the exposure before controls; residual risk is what remains after controls are applied and should be compared to risk appetite.
questions.explanation: Inherent risk is the level of exposure before considering controls; residual risk is what remains after controls operate, and it is the residual figure that management compares to appetite to decide on further treatment. They are not equal when controls have effect, and while residual is normally below inherent, poorly designed or failed controls can leave residual effectively unchanged — so 'never higher' is not a reliable absolute.

questions.q: An emerging technology is being adopted rapidly across business units without central oversight ('shadow IT'). What is the risk practitioner's BEST first action?
choices: Identify and assess where and how the technology is used so the actual exposure can be understood before recommending treatment.
Immediately ban all use of the technology company-wide.
Ignore it because business units accept their own risk.
Purchase cyber insurance to cover any resulting loss.
questions.explanation: You cannot treat what you have not measured; the first step is to discover and assess the shadow-IT usage and its exposure, then recommend proportionate treatment. An immediate blanket ban may be infeasible and drive usage further underground, business-unit acceptance does not remove enterprise accountability, and buying insurance is a transfer decision that should follow — not precede — understanding the risk.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A newly appointed risk practitioner is asked to build an IT risk management program from scratch. Which of the following should be established FIRST?
choices: An IT risk register populated with the top ten technology risks
A board-approved risk appetite and tolerance statement
A library of key risk indicators (KRIs) for each business unit
A control self-assessment (CSA) calendar for application owners
questions.explanation: CRISC treats the risk appetite and tolerance statement as the cornerstone of any IT risk program: without a board-endorsed definition of how much risk the enterprise is willing to accept, the practitioner has no benchmark for prioritising risks, evaluating responses, or escalating exceptions. The risk register, KRI library and CSA calendar are downstream artefacts that must be calibrated against the appetite once it exists.

questions.q: An organisation is finalising its IT risk management framework. Who is ULTIMATELY accountable for the enterprise's IT risk decisions?
choices: The chief information security officer (CISO)
The chief risk officer (CRO)
The board of directors
The IT risk management committee
questions.explanation: Under CRISC and broader corporate-governance principles, accountability for risk cannot be delegated: it rests with the board of directors. The CRO, CISO and risk committee execute and report on risk activities, but the board owns the risk appetite, approves the framework, and remains accountable to shareholders and regulators for the enterprise's overall risk posture.

questions.q: A risk practitioner is preparing the quarterly IT risk report for the board. Which content is MOST valuable to include?
choices: A complete inventory of every open vulnerability across all systems
Top risks against appetite, trend movement, status of mitigation actions, and out-of-tolerance items requiring board attention
Detailed technical descriptions of recent security incidents
Vendor product comparisons for the next year's security tooling
questions.explanation: Board-level risk reporting must be concise, decision-oriented and aligned to risk appetite. CRISC guidance highlights four reporting essentials: the top risks relative to appetite, how they are trending, the status of agreed mitigation actions, and any items breaching tolerance that require board decisions. Raw vulnerability lists, technical incident detail and product comparisons belong in management and operational reporting layers, not the boardroom.

questions.q: The board asks for risk reporting that helps them make decisions. Which reporting practice BEST serves that need?
choices: Concise reporting that relates key risks to business objectives, shows trend against appetite/tolerance, and highlights items needing a decision.
A raw export of every entry in the risk register.
A monthly count of firewall alerts.
Technical vulnerability scan output with CVSS scores only.
questions.explanation: Board-level risk reporting should connect the most significant risks to business objectives, show movement against appetite and tolerance, and flag decisions the board must make — decision-useful and concise. A full register dump, firewall alert counts, or raw CVSS scan output are operational detail that obscures rather than informs strategic decisions.

questions.q: An organisation's recovery time objective (RTO) for its order-entry system is 4 hours, and the recovery point objective (RPO) is 1 hour. Which combination of capabilities BEST supports these objectives?
choices: Daily full backups stored offsite and a cold disaster recovery site
Hourly transaction-log shipping to a warm standby site with documented failover procedures
Weekly backups and a contractual agreement for hardware delivery within 72 hours
Monthly snapshot backups and manual rebuild procedures
questions.explanation: An RPO of 1 hour means no more than 1 hour of data loss is tolerable, requiring backup or replication at least hourly — transaction-log shipping meets this. An RTO of 4 hours means systems must be operational within 4 hours, which a warm standby site with prepared procedures can deliver. Cold sites and hardware-delivery contracts cannot meet a 4-hour RTO, and daily/weekly/monthly backup cadences violate the 1-hour RPO.

questions.q: A third-party vendor will process sensitive customer data on behalf of the organisation. Which statement about risk responsibility is CORRECT?
choices: Outsourcing the processing transfers all data-protection accountability to the vendor
The organisation retains accountability for the risk even though some control activities are operated by the vendor
The vendor's certifications (e.g. ISO 27001, SOC 2) eliminate the need for any oversight
Risk responsibility shifts entirely to the vendor only once a signed contract is in place
questions.explanation: A core CRISC principle — reinforced by regulations such as GDPR — is that accountability for risk cannot be outsourced even when execution is. The organisation remains the data controller and answerable to customers and regulators; the vendor is the operator of certain controls. Vendor certifications inform due diligence but do not replace ongoing oversight, contract clauses, monitoring, and exit planning that the practitioner is expected to embed in third-party risk management.
